documents.extractedText:
KOCHI METRO RAIL LIMITED
HUMAN RESOURCES & EMPLOYEE WELFARE DIVISION
CIRCULAR NO:
KMRL/HR/BONUS/2026/019
DATE: 24 October 2026
CATEGORY: HR POLICY
POLICY CIRCULAR: ANNUAL PERFORMANCE LINKED
INCENTIVE (PLI) & DIWALI FESTIVAL BONUS — FY 2025–26
Applicable to All Regular Employees, Station Controllers, Maintenance Technicians & Executive
Cadres
Sanction Ref: KMRL-MD-RES-2026-88 Eligibility Cutoff: 31 March 2026
Disbursement Date: 28 October
2026
1. Scope & Objective
Kochi Metro Rail Limited (KMRL) is pleased to announce the disbursement schedule and qualifying criteria for the Annual
Performance-Linked Incentive (PLI) and Festival Ex-Gratia for the fiscal year 2025–26, approved in the 68th Board of
Directors session.
2. Incentive Structure & Payout Bands
Cadre / Level Annual Rating Threshold Basic Multiplier Ex-Gratia Amount
Executive (E1 - E6) Score >= 4.2 / 5.0 (Exceeds) 1.5x Basic Pay Rs. 25,000 (Fixed Cap)
Supervisors (S1 - S3) Score >= 3.8 / 5.0 (Commendable) 1.75x Basic Pay Rs. 22,500 (Fixed Cap)
Non-Executive / Operators Satisfactory Attendance (> 92%) 2.0x Basic Pay Rs. 20,000 (Flat Bonus)
Contracted Auxiliary Staff Active tenure > 180 days N/A Rs. 7,500 (Festival Gift)
3. Claim Process & Verification
• Automated Payroll Credit: Eligible employees will receive credit directly in their registered State Bank of India (SBI)
salary accounts alongside the October 2026 payroll run.
• Appraisal Grievances: Any rating dispute must be logged via the KMRL IDMS Employee Portal before 26 October
2026, 17:00 IST.
Issued By:
Gunjan R.
General Manager (Human Resources)
Financial Concurrence:
Finance & Accounts Cell
KMRL Corporate HQ, Ernakulam
By Order of:
Managing Director

documents.extractedText:
KOCHI METRO RAIL LIMITED
OPERATIONS & SAFETY DIVISION — MUTTOM OCC
REF: KMRL/OPS/SOP/2026/042
DATE: 24 October 2026
STATUS: OFFICIAL DRAFT
STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE: MONSOON
READINESS & ELEVATED VIADUCT SAFETY DIRECTIVE
(2026–2027)
Mandatory Compliance Guidelines for Train Operators, OCC Controllers & P-Way Engineers
Document ID: KMRL-SOP-2026-042 Security Level: Restricted / Departmental Revision: 3.2 (Final)
Issuing Authority: Director of Rolling
Stock Corridor: Aluva – Petta – SN Junction Effective Date: Immediate Effect
1. Executive Summary & Purpose
In accordance with Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) seasonal advisories and the Metro Railways
(Operation and Maintenance) Act, this directive establishes fail-safe protocols governing metro train operations, viaduct
water drainage, automatic signaling attenuation, and 750V DC traction isolation across all 25 operational stations.
2. Severe Weather Speed Restrictions & Automatic Train Protection (ATP)
Train operators and automatic driving modes must dynamically adhere to the following precipitation thresholds:
Weather Condition Visibility Range Operating Mode Max Speed
Normal / Light Showers > 500 meters Auto Mode (ATO) 80 km/h
Moderate Monsoon Rain 200m – 500m Coded Manual (CM) 60 km/h
Heavy Downpour / Squall 100m – 200m Restricted Manual (RM) 45 km/h
Severe Storm (Wind > 70 km/h) < 100 meters OCC Caution Order 25 km/h
3. 750V DC Third Rail Traction & Drainage Integrity
• Scupper Drain Inspections: All viaduct downpipes and pier drainage basins between Kalamassery and Muttom
depot must be inspected every 48 hours to prevent standing water.
• Third Rail Clearance: If standing water reaches within 50mm of the bottom shroud of the 750V DC bottom-contact
third rail conductor, OCC must immediately execute controlled traction isolation.
• ATC Balise Verification: Post-flash flooding, signal engineers must execute transmission loopback tests on balise
markers at turnaround sidings prior to passenger re-entry.

documents.title: ChestXray DenseNet121 IEEE Paper
documents.extractedText:
Multi-Label Chest X-Ray Disease Detection with
DenseNet121: Per-Disease Threshold Evaluation and
Error Analysis on 14 Thoracic Pathologies
Manish Sable
Dept. of Electronics and Computer Science
Vidyalankar Institute of Technology
Mumbai, India
Sujal Pujari
Dept. of Electronics and Computer Science
Vidyalankar Institute of Technology
Mumbai, India
Vaishnavi Kadam
Dept. of Electronics and Computer Science
Vidyalankar Institute of Technology
Mumbai, India
Abstract—Chest X-rays are read in large numbers every day, a single
image can show several diseases at once, and some findings appear in
only a handful of cases. We trained a DenseNet121 model, built on the
TorchXRayVision library, to detect 14 thoracic diseases from one
chest X-ray. The 5,606 images were split into 3,906 for training, 837
for validation and 863 held out for testing, and each disease received its
own decision threshold chosen on the validation set. On the validation
images, 69.23% (about 580 of 837) had all 14 labels predicted
correctly. Recall was at least 0.80 for every disease and ROC-AUC
ranged from 0.871 to 0.940, but precision ranged from 0.265 (fibrosis)
to 0.839 (infiltration). Across the 14 confusion matrices the model
made 96 false negatives and 336 false positives, so it leans toward
catching disease at the cost of false alarms, and precision tends to be
higher for more common diseases. While checking our results we
found that some exported aggregate metrics do not match the per-
disease rows, so we report both. We also describe the limits of this
evidence, mainly that the thresholds were tuned on the validation
images and that some diseases have very few positive cases.
Index Terms—chest radiography, multi-label classification,
DenseNet121, TorchXRayVision, per-disease threshold, confusion
matrix, class imbalance, medical image analysis
I. INTRODUCTION
Chest radiography is the most common diagnostic imaging
examination, and every radiograph must be read for subtle,
overlapping findings such as small pneumothoraces, early
consolidation or mild cardiomegaly. A shortage of radiologists
and growing workloads delay reports, which motivates
decision-support tools that flag likely abnormalities and help
prioritise urgent cases [1], [2].
The task is a multi-label problem. One image may carry no
finding, one finding or several, so each disease is an
independent binary decision rather than one class among many.
This creates three practical difficulties. Class imbalance is
severe: in our validation set infiltration is positive in 18.2% of
images, whereas hernia is positive in 0.2%. A single 0.5
threshold suits rare diseases poorly, so thresholds must be
chosen per disease. And headline accuracy is misleading,
because with so many negatives a weak model still scores
highly; precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and average precision
must be read together [12].
In this paper we train a DenseNet121 [4] model on top of
TorchXRayVision [5] to detect 14 thoracic diseases and study
its errors one disease at a time. Our contributions are: (1) a 14-
label chest X-ray classifier trained on 3,906 images; (2) a
3,906/837/863 split in which the validation images choose per-
disease thresholds and the test images stay untouched; (3) a per-
disease evaluation that gives confusion-matrix counts together
with precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and average precision; (4)
an analysis showing that the model favours recall and that its
precision follows how common each disease is; and (5) a check
of the exported metric tables against the confusion matrices.
The evaluation is preliminary, and Section VI lists its limits.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Datasets and Supervised CNNs
ChestX-ray8 provided the first large open hospital chest X-
ray benchmark, with 108,948 frontal images whose multi-label
annotations were mined from radiology reports and a weakly
supervised localisation method based on class activation maps
[1]. CheXNet applied a 121-layer DenseNet to the 112,120-
image ChestX-ray14 set with 14 sigmoid outputs and a binary
cross-entropy loss, and reported a pneumonia F1 of 0.435
against 0.387 for radiologists [2]. CheXpert added explicit
uncertainty labels and compared five policies for handling them
across 224,316 radiographs [3]. PadChest [6] and MIMIC-
CXR-JPG [7] supplied multilingual and report-paired data at
larger scale.
B. Vision-Language Pre-training and Foundation Models
ConVIRT learns image representations by contrasting
radiographs with their paired report text [8]. BioViL adds a
rescaled semantic matching loss to avoid penalising clinically
identical reports and releases a phrase-grounding benchmark
[9], and MedCLIP decouples images from texts using a medical
knowledge base so that unpaired data can be used [10].
CheXagent is an instruction-tuned foundation agent trained on
more than 8.4 million instruction triplets for classification,
grounding and report generation [11]. These models offer label
efficiency and zero-shot classification, but they need far more
compute than a compact classifier, and generative agents can
state findings that are not present.
C. Positioning
Table I summarises the supervised baselines. The present
work sits in this first tier: a lightweight, auditable classifier with
a fixed label set. It is smaller in data than the published
benchmarks, so its figures are context for, not a competitor to,
those results. Its focus is a transparent per-disease evaluation,
including how precision behaves for rare diseases, which
headline ROC-AUC figures tend to hide.

-- 1 of 5 --

TABLE I
SUMMARY OF RELATED SUPERVISED CHEST X-RAY WORK
Ref. Images Backbone Contribution
[1] 108,948 ResNet-50 and
others Open benchmark; CAM localisation
[2] 112,120 DenseNet-121 14 sigmoid outputs; pneumonia F1
0.435
[3] 224,316 DenseNet-121 Uncertainty labels and policies
[7] 377,110 Data resource Paired images and reports
This
work 5,606 DenseNet121 Per-disease thresholds and error
analysis
III. METHODOLOGY
A. Problem Formulation
Let a radiograph be X ∈ ℝH×W×C, where H and W are the
spatial dimensions and C is the channel depth. The target is a
binary vector y = [y1, …, yK] {0,1}	∈ K with K = 14 diseases. The
network produces a logit fk(X) for each disease, and training
minimises the sum of binary cross-entropy losses, with σ the
sigmoid function [2]:
L = −Σk=114 [ yk log σ(fk(X)) + (1 − yk) log(1 − σ(fk(X))) ] (1)
The labels used here are binary, so no uncertainty policy of the
CheXpert type [3] is needed.
B. Model and Pipeline
The backbone is DenseNet121, in which every layer receives
the feature maps of all earlier layers within a dense block. This
reuses features, strengthens gradient flow and keeps the
network compact [4]. The network is obtained through
TorchXRayVision, an open-source library of chest X-ray
datasets, pre-processing utilities and pretrained models [5]. The
output layer has 14 sigmoid units, one per pathology, so several
diseases can be positive for one image. Fig. 1 shows the
pipeline.
Fig. 1. The classification pipeline. Training data fit the weights, validation data
select the per-disease thresholds and report metrics, and the test set is held out.
C. Per-Disease Thresholds
A probability is converted to a label by comparing it with a
threshold τk chosen separately for each disease on the validation
set. The selected thresholds are low, from 0.01 for hernia to 0.16
for infiltration, with most between 0.05 and 0.10. A low
threshold flags a disease even when the model is only
moderately confident, which raises recall at the cost of
precision. This is a deliberate choice for a screening aid, where a
missed disease costs more than an extra review.
D. Evaluation Metrics
For each disease the confusion matrix gives true positives
(TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN) and true
negatives (TN):
Precision = TP / (TP + FP), Recall = TP / (TP + FN) (2)
F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) (3)
ROC-AUC measures how well the scores rank positives above
negatives, independently of the threshold. Average precision
(AP) is the area under the precision–recall curve and is more
informative than ROC-AUC when positives are rare [12].
Macro averages weight all 14 diseases equally, while micro
averages pool all image–label decisions. Exact-match accuracy
is the fraction of images with all 14 labels correct, and
Hamming accuracy is the fraction of individual image–label
decisions that are correct.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
A. Dataset and Split
The dataset contains 5,606 chest radiographs labelled with
the 14 pathologies atelectasis, cardiomegaly, effusion,
infiltration, mass, nodule, pneumonia, pneumothorax,
consolidation, edema, emphysema, fibrosis, pleural thickening
and hernia. It is divided as in Table II, roughly 70/15/15. The
training set only fits the weights, the validation set guides
threshold selection and development, and the test set is reserved
for one final evaluation.
TABLE II
DATASET SPLIT
Split Images Share Purpose
Training 3,906 69.7% Learn disease patterns
Validation 837 14.9% Tune thresholds; evaluate during
development
Testing 863 15.4% Final evaluation on held-out data
Total 5,606 100% All three splits combined
In the 837 validation images the number of positive cases per
disease ranges from 152 (infiltration, 18.2%) and 107 (effusion,
12.8%) down to 13 (pneumonia), 11 (fibrosis) and only 2
(hernia). Metrics for the last three diseases rest on very few
examples.
B. Training Configuration
Training follows the reference pipeline of TorchXRayVision
[5]. Radiographs are centre-cropped to a square, resized to
224×224 pixels as single-channel images, and intensity-
normalised to the [−1024, 1024] range used by the library’s
pretrained models. The network is DenseNet121 with 14
sigmoid outputs, trained with the binary cross-entropy loss of
(1) (BCEWithLogitsLoss in PyTorch). Weights are updated
with the Adam optimizer (AMSGrad variant, weight decay
10−5) at an initial learning rate of 0.001 and a batch size of 64.
Data augmentation applies random affine transforms with
rotation up to 45°, translation up to 15% and scale change up to

-- 2 of 5 --

15%. The pretrained model is used as the starting point and the
14 outputs are fitted to the labelled training images.
The 837 validation images were not used to update the
weights; they served only to monitor performance during
development and to select the per-disease thresholds, and the
863 test images were kept out of both training and tuning.
C. Evaluation Protocol
All results in Section V are computed on the 837 validation
images. Thresholds were selected on the same images, so the
reported figures are optimistic, and the 863-image test set has
not been used for any reported number. Precision, recall,
thresholds, ROC-AUC and AP are taken from the exported
validation report; F1 is recomputed from the confusion-matrix
counts using (3); and pooled counts are summed over the 14
matrices.
V. RESULTS
A. Aggregate Performance
Table III lists the aggregate metrics. Of the 837 validation
images, 69.23% (about 580) have all 14 labels predicted
correctly, and 94.12% of individual decisions are correct
according to the exported report. The macro ROC-AUC is
0.8842, which indicates good overall separation of positive
from negative cases. The table also gives the same quantities
recomputed from the per-class rows, because several exported
aggregates differ from them; Section VI-B discusses this.
TABLE III
AGGREGATE VALIDATION METRICS
Metric Exported From per-class
Exact-match accuracy 0.6923 —
Hamming accuracy 0.9412 0.963
Macro ROC-AUC 0.8842 0.904
Macro average precision 0.5410 0.567
Macro precision 0.6120 0.538
Macro recall 0.7680 0.843
Macro F1 0.6880 0.642
Micro precision 0.5980 0.601
Micro recall 0.7710 0.840
Micro F1 0.6734 0.701
B. Class-Wise Evaluation
Table IV gives the per-disease results and Fig. 2 compares
precision with recall. Recall is between 0.800 and 1.000 for
every disease. Precision is highest for infiltration (0.839),
effusion (0.744) and pneumonia (0.733) and lowest for fibrosis
(0.265), emphysema (0.386) and hernia (0.333). ROC-AUC lies
between 0.871 (nodule) and 0.940 (hernia). Average precision
is much lower than ROC-AUC, from 0.310 to 0.810, because
negatives greatly outnumber positives.
TABLE IV
CLASS-WISE VALIDATION RESULTS
Disease Pos. Prec. Rec. F1 AUC AP
Atelectasis 68 0.675 0.824 0.742 0.892 0.690
Cardiomegaly 17 0.560 0.824 0.667 0.910 0.610
Effusion 107 0.744 0.869 0.802 0.921 0.785
Infiltration 152 0.839 0.855 0.847 0.898 0.810
Mass 46 0.507 0.804 0.622 0.887 0.520
Nodule 48 0.471 0.833 0.602 0.871 0.490
Pneumonia 13 0.733 0.846 0.786 0.932 0.750
Pneumothorax 38 0.604 0.842 0.703 0.914 0.620
Consolidation 30 0.429 0.800 0.558 0.890 0.450
Edema 17 0.538 0.824 0.651 0.925 0.590
Emphysema 27 0.386 0.815 0.524 0.894 0.420
Fibrosis 11 0.265 0.818 0.400 0.880 0.310
Pleural Thick. 26 0.449 0.846 0.587 0.895 0.480
Hernia 2 0.333 1.000 0.500 0.940 0.410
Pos. = positive images among 837. AUC = ROC-AUC; AP = average precision. F1 is
recomputed from the confusion matrices. Pleural thickening appears twice in the exported
report with AP 0.480 and 0.410; the first value is used.
Fig. 2. Per-disease precision and recall on the validation set.
C. Confusion Matrices
Fig. 3 shows the per-disease confusion matrices. Summed
over the 14 diseases there are 506 true positives, 96 false
negatives, 336 false positives and 10,780 true negatives, out of
11,718 image–label decisions. Missed cases are few:
pneumothorax has 6 false negatives among 38 positives, and
fibrosis 2 among 11. Most errors are false alarms, and nodule
(45) and mass (36) produce the most of them. The F1 values
printed above the panels in Fig. 3 are those of the exported
figure and do not equal the F1 in Table IV (Section VI-B).

-- 3 of 5 --

Fig. 3. Per-disease confusion matrices of DenseNet121 on the validation set (full width for legibility).
D. Precision and Prevalence
Fig. 4 plots precision against validation prevalence. The two
are positively correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.59, n = 14, p = 0.025):
common diseases such as infiltration and effusion reach higher
precision, whereas the rarest diseases fall below 0.45. This is
expected, since at a fixed score distribution a lower prevalence
means a larger share of false positives among all flagged cases.
Fig. 4. Precision against validation prevalence (log scale).
VI. DISCUSSION
A. Interpretation
The model is recall-oriented. With low thresholds, every
disease reaches recall of at least 0.80 and only 96 positives are
missed against 506 found, so it suits a triage or second-reader
role in which a missed finding is more costly than an
unnecessary review. The high ROC-AUC values (0.871 to
0.940) show that the underlying scores rank diseased images
well, and the lower AP values show that this ranking does not
translate into high precision for rare diseases. The weakest
classes (fibrosis, emphysema, consolidation) combine low
prevalence with findings that are diffuse or easily confused with
normal structures.
Published baselines give context only. CheXNet reported a
mean AUC of 0.841 over the 14 ChestX-ray14 pathologies [2],
and the original ChestX-ray8 baseline about 0.745 over eight
pathologies [1]. Our per-class mean ROC-AUC of 0.904 (0.884
as exported) is in a similar range, but the datasets, sizes
(112,120 versus 5,606 images) and splits differ, and our figure
comes from a validation set that also selected the thresholds, so
the numbers are not directly comparable.

-- 4 of 5 --

B. Consistency of the Exported Metrics
Recomputing the metrics from the confusion matrices
exposed mismatches with the exported summary. The F1 values
of 0.77 to 0.81 printed in the report and on the matrix panels
cannot be obtained from the listed precision and recall: for
atelectasis, precision 0.675 and recall 0.824 give F1 = 0.742, not
0.79. The macro averages in the summary also differ from the
means of the per-class rows (Table III), and the confusion
matrices imply a Hamming accuracy of about 0.963 against the
exported 0.941. The class-wise table lists pleural thickening
twice with different AP values. These differences suggest that
summary and per-class figures came from different runs or
thresholds, and all tables should be regenerated from one script
and one saved set of predictions before the results are treated as
final.
C. What the Results Show and Do Not Show
The results show that a DenseNet121 with per-disease
thresholds can detect 14 pathologies with high sensitivity and
good score separation on this dataset. They do not show general
performance. The thresholds and metrics use the same 837
images; the test set is not reported; hernia, fibrosis and
pneumonia have 2, 11 and 13 positives, so a single changed
prediction would alter their scores markedly; there is a single
split with no confidence intervals; and there is no independent
baseline trained on the same split. The data are from a single
source, so generalisation to other hospitals, scanners and
populations is untested. Chest radiographs are also personal
medical data, and any deployment would need clinical
validation and privacy safeguards.
VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE
We trained a DenseNet121 classifier on 3,906 chest X-rays,
tuned it on 837 validation images and kept 863 images for
testing. On the validation set it found at least 80% of the positive
cases for every disease, with ROC-AUC between 0.871 and
0.940. Its weak point is precision: it raised 336 false alarms
against 96 missed cases, and the rarest and most diffuse findings
suffered most. Checking the exported tables against the
confusion matrices also showed inconsistencies that need to be
fixed. Overall, the results show that the approach is feasible as a
triage aid, but they do not establish clinical accuracy.
Several steps remain. We need to report test-set results with
the thresholds fixed, regenerate every metric from one script,
and add bootstrap confidence intervals, particularly for the rare
diseases. To improve precision without losing recall we plan to
try class-balanced or focal loss and oversampling, and to choose
thresholds on a separate calibration split. Starting from a vision-
language pre-trained encoder [8]–[10], adding Grad-CAM
maps to confirm that predictions come from the right lung
regions, comparing with independent baselines on the same
split, and validating on data from another hospital would also
strengthen the work.
ACKNOWLEDGMENT
The authors thank the Department of Electronics and
Computer Science, Vidyalankar Institute of Technology,
Mumbai, for its support, and Prof. Faiz Rangari for guidance.
Parts of the manuscript text and figures were prepared with the
help of an AI language model (Anthropic Claude); the authors
reviewed and edited all content and take responsibility for it.
REFERENCES
[1] X. Wang, Y. Peng, L. Lu, Z. Lu, M. Bagheri, and R. M. Summers,
“ChestX-ray8: Hospital-scale chest X-ray database and benchmarks on
weakly-supervised classification and localization of common thorax
diseases,” in Proc. IEEE Conf. Comput. Vis. Pattern Recognit. (CVPR),
2017, pp. 2097–2106.
[2] P. Rajpurkar et al., “CheXNet: Radiologist-level pneumonia detection on
chest X-rays with deep learning,” 2017, arXiv:1711.05225.
[3] J. Irvin et al., “CheXpert: A large chest radiograph dataset with
uncertainty labels and expert comparison,” in Proc. AAAI Conf. Artif.
Intell., vol. 33, no. 1, 2019, pp. 590–597.
[4] G. Huang, Z. Liu, L. van der Maaten, and K. Q. Weinberger, “Densely
connected convolutional networks,” in Proc. IEEE Conf. Comput. Vis.
Pattern Recognit. (CVPR), 2017, pp. 4700–4708.
[5] J. P. Cohen et al., “TorchXRayVision: A library of chest X-ray datasets
and models,” in Proc. Med. Imaging Deep Learn. (MIDL), 2022.
[6] A. Bustos, A. Pertusa, J.-M. Salinas, and M. de la Iglesia-Vayá,
“PadChest: A large chest x-ray image dataset with multi-label annotated
reports,” 2019, arXiv:1901.07441.
[7] A. E. W. Johnson et al., “MIMIC-CXR-JPG, a large publicly available
database of labeled chest radiographs,” 2019, arXiv:1901.07042.
[8] Y. Zhang, H. Jiang, Y. Miura, C. D. Manning, and C. P. Langlotz,
“Contrastive learning of medical visual representations from paired
images and text,” 2020, arXiv:2010.00747.
[9] B. Boecking et al., “Making the most of text semantics to improve
biomedical vision–language processing,” in Proc. Eur. Conf. Comput.
Vis. (ECCV), 2022.
[10] Z. Wang, Z. Wu, D. Agarwal, and J. Sun, “MedCLIP: Contrastive learning
from unpaired medical images and text,” in Proc. Conf. Empirical
Methods Natural Lang. Process. (EMNLP), 2022, pp. 3876–3887.
[11] Z. Chen et al., “CheXagent: Towards a foundation model for chest X-ray
interpretation,” 2024, arXiv:2401.12208.
[12] T. Saito and M. Rehmsmeier, “The precision-recall plot is more
informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on
imbalanced datasets,” PLoS ONE, vol. 10, no. 3, p. e0118432, 2015.
